clinical_category: Oncology psychosocial care - acute distress after diagnosis
stem: A client who has just been told of a new cancer diagnosis says, 'After I heard the word cancer, I stopped hearing anything else. I cannot think straight.' Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.A: Acknowledge the client's distress, assess what the client understands and needs now, and review important information in small amounts with opportunities to repeat and clarify it while offering psychosocial support as needed.
options.B: Provide all treatment details immediately in one uninterrupted session because emotional distress should not change how information is communicated.
options.C: Reassure the client that there is no reason to be frightened and redirect the conversation away from emotional concerns.
options.D: Give all future information only to the family because acute distress means the client can no longer participate in health care decisions.

rationale: A is correct. NCI notes that a new cancer diagnosis can produce heightened distress that impairs attention and cognitive processing. NCI communication guidance recommends responding to emotion, limiting emotionally charged information at each interaction, repeating important information, checking understanding, and avoiding long detailed explanations when the patient is not ready to absorb them. Psychosocial assessment and referral are appropriate when clinically significant distress is identified. B risks information overload. C uses premature reassurance and dismisses the client's expressed emotion. D unnecessarily removes the client from communication and decision-making rather than adapting communication to the client's current needs and preferences.
educational_objective: Respond therapeutically to acute distress after a cancer diagnosis by validating emotion, assessing understanding and support needs, and pacing/repeating information to preserve comprehension and participation in care.
source_organization: National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health
source_document_title: Adjustment to Cancer: Anxiety and Distress (PDQ®) — Health Professional Version; Communication in Cancer Care (PDQ®) — Health Professional Version and Patient Version
source_version_date: Current NCI PDQ resources accessed 2026-08-18; Communication in Cancer Care patient version updated 2025-04-07
source_locator: Adjustment to Cancer HP PDQ — 'Psychosocial Assessment' and 'Situation-Specific Influences on Adjustment' → 'Hearing the diagnosis', including heightened distress impairing attention/cognitive processing and referral/support; Communication in Cancer Care HP PDQ — 'Informational Versus Emotional Aspects of Communication', low-health-literacy communication recommendations to limit emotionally charged information and repeat important information, Ask-Tell-Ask guidance using small chunks/checking understanding, and 'Diagnostic Disclosure and Breaking Bad News' warning against premature reassurance; Patient Version — 'Factors in Communication' and suggestions for remembering information.
source_claim_supported: Distress around diagnosis can impair attention and information processing; communication should acknowledge emotion, limit information per interaction, repeat/check understanding, and connect clients with psychosocial support when distress warrants it.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Client Needs category 'Psychosocial Integrity' — nursing care that promotes and supports emotional, mental and social well-being; applied here to therapeutic communication, coping assessment and psychosocial support after a serious diagnosis.
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source's low-discrimination list of possible emotions into an applied therapeutic-communication scenario. The final item directly tests NCI-supported effects of acute distress on information processing and appropriate paced, validating communication without false reassurance or loss of autonomy.
audit_findings: Fresh NCI review directly supports that heightened distress after diagnosis can impair attention and cognitive processing.
NCI communication guidance directly supports limiting emotionally charged information per interaction, repeating important information, checking comprehension and responding to emotion.
The key preserves the client's autonomy and adapts communication rather than transferring decisions to family solely because of acute distress.
Distractors are clinically realistic errors: information overload, premature reassurance and inappropriate exclusion of the client.
